meta.title: The potential adverse effects of hypodermic glucagon-like peptide -1 receptor agonist on patients with type 2 diabetes: A population-based study.
meta.abstract:
Background

Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs), a class of injectable antidiabetic drugs, have shown significant efficacies in improving glycemic and weight control in patients with type 2 diabetes (T2D). However, the long-term safety of GLP-1 RAs remains insufficiently studied. This study aimed to provide real-world evidence on potential adverse outcomes associated with GLP-1 RAs use in T2D patients without major chronic diseases including impaired cardiac or renal function.

Methods

We conducted a retrospective cohort study involving 7746 T2D patients on GLP-1 RAs in Shenzhen, China. They were compared with 124 371 metformin-only users and 36 146 insulin-only users, forming two therapy control groups. GLP-1 RAs users were also further 1:2 paired with the control groups. Competing risk survival analyses were conducted to assess the incidence risks, presenting subdistributional hazard ratios (sHRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for various adverse outcomes associated with GLP-1 RAs use.

Results

Compared with metformin-only users, GLP-1 RAs use was associated with increased risks of various adverse outcomes (sHRs with 95% CIs), including pancreatitis (2.01, 1.24-3.24), acute nephritis (3.20, 2.17-4.70), kidney failure (3.73, 2.74-5.08), thyroid cancer (2.25, 1.23-4.10), and thyroid dysfunction (1.27, 1.00-1.63), respectively; Similar results were also found when compared with insulin-only users. Importantly, long-term (≥12 months) GLP-1 RAs use may further elevate the incidence risks of pancreatitis, acute nephritis, thyroid cancer, and thyroid dysfunction.

Conclusion

Compared with traditional T2D treatments, GLP-1 RAs use may be associated with increased risks of various adverse outcomes in a Chinese population. Cautions were strongly warranted in the use of GLP-1 RAs. Further validation is crucial across diverse populations.

domains.name: Confounding
domains.direction_justification: GLP-1 RA users had higher baseline obesity (BMI 30.0-39.9 kg/m²: 13.21% vs 3.04% in insulin and 4.87% in metformin) and higher socioeconomic/insurance coverage (Citizen health insurance: 75.60% vs 59.60% in insulin and 54.96% in metformin) prior to matching. Critical clinical confounders including duration of diabetes, baseline renal function (eGFR, proteinuria), baseline triglycerides, and glycemic control (HbA1c missing in 91.27% of patients) were unadjusted, exaggerating risk estimates away from the null.

findings.title: Confounding by indication and disease severity
findings.mechanism: Comparing GLP-1 RA users to metformin-only (mild/early T2D) and insulin-only (advanced beta-cell failure) introduces severe indication bias. GLP-1 RAs are prescribed to distinct patient profiles with differing metabolic and organ vulnerability.
evidence: Baseline BMI 30.0-39.9 kg/m2 was 13.21% in GLP-1 RAs vs 4.87% in metformin and 3.04% in insulin
HbA1c missingness was 91.27% across groups, preventing adjustment for baseline glycemic control
Fasting plasma glucose missing rate was 33.22%

findings.title: Inadequate adjustment through missing-category indicator matching
findings.mechanism: Propensity score matching included 'unspecified' as a valid matching category for BMI (33.81% missing in GLP-1 group), education (33.62% missing), and age (20.53% missing), matching on missingness patterns rather than balancing true underlying confounder distributions.

domains.name: Measurement of the exposure
domains.direction_justification: Exposure was determined via electronic prescription records without confirmation of dispensing, actual subcutaneous injection adherence, or dosage, leading to non-differential exposure misclassification that typically biases estimates towards the null.

findings.title: Prescription record proxy without adherence validation
findings.mechanism: Defining exposure by cumulative prescription coverage rather than verified medication dispensing or patient adherence misclassifies non-adherent patients as exposed.
evidence: Exposure defined as patients mainly prescribed GLP-1 RAs lasting from baseline to last follow-up with other antidiabetic prescriptions <6 months
No data on prescription fulfillment, dose titration, or administration compliance

findings.title: Immortal and post-hoc exposure classification bias
findings.mechanism: Defining cohorts by predominant therapy accrued from baseline to the end of follow-up introduces conditioning on the future, misaligning baseline covariate assessment and follow-up start.
evidence: The GLP‐1 RAs group was defined as any T2D patients who mainly prescribed GLP‐1 RAs lasting from the baseline date to the last follow‐up while the accumulative prescription period of any other antidiabetic medication <6 months.

findings.title: Absence of washout period (Prevalent-user bias)
findings.mechanism: Without a lookback/washout period to restrict to incident new users, prevalent users who have already tolerated the drug are mixed with new users.
evidence: Washout period was not reported in the methods.

findings.title: Absence of latency lag period for chronic/oncologic outcomes
findings.mechanism: Failing to lag exposure allows pre-existing subclinical diseases (e.g., thyroid cancer diagnosed within months of prescription) to be attributed to the drug, introducing reverse causation and detection bias.
evidence: All incidence duration/survival times for outcomes of interest were operationalized as the number of months from the initial outpatient date at baseline to the occurrence of the first recorded hospitalization/outpatient events, whichever came first.

domains.name: Selection of participants into the study
domains.direction_justification: Requiring patients to maintain predominant monotherapy (<6 months of other antidiabetic drugs) across the entire follow-up period conditions inclusion on future post-baseline treatment trajectories, introducing immortal time and survivorship selection bias.

findings.title: Conditioning cohort entry on post-baseline treatment persistence
findings.mechanism: Defining groups based on prescription duration from baseline date to last follow-up creates artificial monotherapy cohorts that do not reflect clinical practice and selects for specific disease trajectories.
evidence: 362,035 out of 985,278 patients (36.7%) were excluded due to missing prescription data
GLP-1 RA group required cumulative prescription of any other antidiabetic medication <6 months over total follow-up

domains.name: Post-exposure interventions
domains.direction_justification: Concomitant medications (such as ACE inhibitors, ARBs, statins, or NSAIDs) and therapy switches during the follow-up period were not tracked or adjusted over time, making the net direction of bias unpredictable.

findings.title: Unmeasured concomitant co-interventions and competing risks handling
findings.mechanism: Systematically defining acute side effects (e.g. diarrhea, vomiting, dizziness) as competing events that censor follow-up can distort subdistribution hazard ratios for downstream chronic events.
evidence: Competing risks systematically activated by incidence of acute symptoms including diarrhea/emesis, tetter, acne, dizziness, arrhythmia

domains.name: Missing data
domains.direction_justification: Extensive missingness in primary clinical parameters (HbA1c missing in 91.27%, FPG missing in 33.22%, BMI missing in 32.49-33.81%) handled via dummy variable categorization masks severe residual confounding by metabolic derangement and obesity, biasing hazard ratios away from the null.

findings.title: Extreme missingness in key physiological variables
findings.mechanism: Over 90% missingness in HbA1c and >30% missingness in FPG and BMI prevents effective adjustment for metabolic control, confounding observed associations with renal and pancreatic outcomes.
evidence: HbA1c missing rate was 91.27% (Table 1 footnote)
Fasting plasma glucose missing rate was 33.22% (Table 1 footnote)
BMI was unspecified in 33.81% of GLP-1 RA users and 36.08% of insulin users

domains.name: Measurement of the outcome
domains.direction_justification: Patients initiated on newer injectable GLP-1 RAs receive substantially more clinical surveillance, laboratory workups (e.g. amylase/lipase, thyroid ultrasound, renal function panels), and specialist visits than stable metformin users, inflating detection of subclinical or mild outcomes (e.g. thyroid dysfunction sHR 1.27, acute nephritis sHR 3.20, pancreatitis sHR 2.01).

findings.title: Surveillance and diagnostic workup bias
findings.mechanism: Outcomes identified via ICD-10 and text string regular expressions from routine outpatient/inpatient electronic records without standardized blinding or independent adjudication are highly sensitive to differential surveillance intensity.
evidence: Outcomes identified using regular expression matching and ICD-10 from routine outpatient and inpatient records (Table 2S)
GLP-1 RA users had significantly higher citizen health insurance coverage (75.60% vs 54.96% in metformin) facilitating more frequent hospital visits

domains.name: Selection of the reported result
domains.direction_justification: Multiple outcomes and subgroup comparisons (stratified by 12-month usage and individual agents) were evaluated without a pre-registered prospective statistical analysis protocol or multiplicity correction, favouring reporting of extreme hazard ratios (e.g., leukemia sHR 15.09, 95% CI 4.65-48.98).

findings.title: Multiple outcome testing without multiplicity control
findings.mechanism: Evaluating numerous organ systems and duration strata without family-wise error rate control increases the likelihood of finding and emphasizing statistically significant positive associations.
evidence: Over 15 distinct clinical endpoints evaluated across multiple duration strata and 4 individual GLP-1 RA agents
Extreme effect estimates highlighted for rare events (leukemia sHR 15.09, 95% CI: 4.65-48.98)

overall.summary: The study is at very high risk of bias across multiple ROBINS-E domains, primarily driven by severe confounding by indication, pervasive missing baseline data (HbA1c missing in 91.27% of participants, BMI missing in ~33%), selection bias from conditioning cohort membership on post-baseline prescription trajectories, and differential surveillance/detection bias between patients on newer injectable GLP-1 RAs versus oral metformin. Propensity score matching on 'unspecified' missing categories failed to control for baseline disease severity. Consequently, the observed elevated risks (e.g., acute nephritis, kidney failure, pancreatitis, leukemia) cannot be interpreted as causal drug effects.

unresolvable_without_more_data: Raw event counts for each adverse outcome in the exposed and control groups (only sHRs and 95% CIs are reported in the text/figures).
Baseline renal laboratory parameters (serum creatinine, eGFR, urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio) to evaluate baseline nephropathy.
Baseline lipid profiles (triglycerides) and alcohol consumption history to evaluate baseline pancreatitis risk.
True missing-data mechanism and complete-case or multiple-imputation analyses for HbA1c, FPG, and BMI.

time_related_biases.summary: The study defines exposure post-hoc based on treatments received throughout follow-up without an incident new-user design or washout period. Furthermore, the absence of a lag period for long-latency outcomes like thyroid cancer and leukemia in a cohort followed for an average of only 23.7 months creates substantial detection bias and reverse causation towards inflated harm estimates.
